checks.location: Lemma3.1, strict concavity of causal entropy on feasible discounted occupancy measures; Appendix A.1
checks.claim: Lemma3.1, strict concavity of causal entropy on feasible discounted occupancy measures; Appendix A.1
checks.explanation: No substantive error in this selected lemma. Policies at unreachable states are only defined up to arbitrary choices; strict uniqueness concerns occupancies. The entire IRL minimax theorem and attainment of unbounded cost optimisation are not certified.
checks.demonstration: The log-sum inequality proves concavity state by state. Equality for an interior mixture requires the same conditional action law wherever both occupancies carry positive state mass. A common compatible policy can then be defined on the union of their supports; both occupancies solve that policy's same discounted linear flow equation, which has a unique solution because I−gamma P is invertible. Thus equality implies equal occupancies, establishing strict concavity on the feasible flow polytope despite conditional entropy not being strictly concave on arbitrary joint measures. The identities H(pi)=Hbar(rho_pi) and Hbar(rho)=H(pi_rho) follow by substituting the conditional action law.

checks.location: Lemma6 and Lemma8 per-type posterior approximation inequalities
checks.claim: for every buyer’s type $k\in\mathcal{K}$
checks.explanation: Optimality after averaging over types does not imply optimality for each type separately. A payment that increases the seller’s total payoff can reduce the seller’s payoff conditional on a minority type. The first typewise comparison in the proof uses precisely this unsupported implication.
checks.demonstration: Take two states with identical utilities, seller rewards \((1,0)\) for actions \((A,B)\), type probabilities \((0.9,0.1)\), and buyer utilities \((0,0)\), \((0,0.5)\). Set grid payments to zero. Their weighted seller payoff is \(0.9\); inducing both types to \(A\) requires an exact differential \(0.5\), giving at most \(0.5\). For Lemma 6 choose \(\alpha=0.1\), \(q=100\), and \(\epsilon=\sqrt{2\log(40)/100}\). The approximate-response threshold is \(0.5-\epsilon\), and \(0.5+\epsilon<0.9\), so zero grid payments remain optimal. At the off-grid posterior \(\xi^*=(\sqrt2/2,1-\sqrt2/2)\), set payment \((0.5,0)\). The minority type gives seller payoff \(0.5\) there and zero at every grid posterior. Every grid mixture therefore violates the required bound \(0\geq0.4\), including every mixture with mean \(\xi^*\). Lemma 8 has the same exact-response failure with \(q=1800\).
checks.repair:
Replace “for every type” by the type-weighted conclusion, with \(\lambda_k\) the type probabilities, \(m\) the number of actions and \(d\) the number of states. Use the paper’s bounds \(u^s,u^k\in[0,1]\).

**Lemma 6.** For \(\epsilon>0\) and \(0<\alpha\leq1\), use an integer \(q\geq\lceil2\log(4m/\alpha)/\epsilon^2\rceil\); the printed logarithmic constant instead yields loss at most \(2\alpha\) by this argument. Freeze the benchmark payment at \(\xi^*\). On each type’s Hoeffding good event its old best action remains \(\epsilon\)-best. Off that event the relative seller loss is at most two, since old buyer optimality implies \(p(b)-p(a_k)\leq1\). Weighting the per-type failure probabilities gives loss at most \(4m e^{-q\epsilon^2/2}\), without a union over types.

**Lemma 8.** Decompose \(\xi^*\) into neighboring \(q\)-grid points of exactly the same mean and coordinate error at most \(1/q\). Put \(\epsilon=2d/q\); the old best actions are then \(\epsilon\)-best. The mixed contract loses at most \(2\sqrt\epsilon\) before the aggregate grid optimizer is applied. Exact-mean averaging of the affine benchmark removes seller-reward drift. With the original \(q=\lceil9d/\alpha^2\rceil\), the total loss is at most \((2\sqrt2/3)\alpha<\alpha\). For \(\alpha>1\), nonnegative optimal aggregate grid payoff and benchmark payoff at most one give the weighted bound directly.
checks.scope: The per-type lemma statements are false. The established local repair is prior-weighted, with the stated constant adjustment for Lemma 6; it does not certify the downstream approximation algorithm.
checks.contextBefore: Lemma 6 uses \(q=2\log(2m/\alpha)/\epsilon^2\), nonnegative posterior-dependent payments and seller-favorable choices among \(\epsilon\)-best responses.
checks.contextAfter: The signaling distribution must also satisfy \(\sum_{\xi\in\Xi_q}\gamma_\xi\xi=\xi^*\).
checks.title: Posterior-optimal payments need not preserve every buyer type
checks.claimContext: Lemma 6 requires the approximation inequality “for every buyer’s type \(k\in\mathcal K\)”; Lemma 8 makes the corresponding assertion for every receiver type. The grid payment maximizes the type-weighted seller objective.
checks.whyItMatters: A guarantee for every buyer type is stronger than a guarantee for the seller’s weighted objective.
checks.checkedLocation: Lemmas 6 and 8; Appendix C, per-type optimality comparison

review-neurips-2026-150804.title: It Just Takes Two: Scaling Amortized Inference to Large Sets

checks.location: Appendix A, Corollary 2 forward implication and Equation (15)
checks.claim: Under listed regularity, additive sufficiency of shared-nuisance marginals implies (15) with eta(theta) and S(x) independent of N.
checks.explanation: A shared nuisance makes the marginal observations dependent. Their fixed-dimensional additive sufficient statistic can have a set-size-dependent likelihood coefficient, contradicting the asserted uniform exponential form.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(X_i=\theta+\psi+\epsilon_i\), with independent \(\psi\sim N(0,\tau^2)\), \(\epsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\), and \(\sigma^2,\tau^2>0\). The marginal is smooth, identifiable, dominated and has full parameter-independent support. Its log likelihood ratio to \(\theta=0\) is

\[
\log\frac{p(X_N\mid\theta)}{p(X_N\mid0)}=\frac{\theta\sum_i x_i}{\sigma^2+N\tau^2}-\frac{N\theta^2}{2(\sigma^2+N\tau^2)}.
\]

The sum is minimal sufficient at every \(N\): a likelihood ratio for two data vectors is parameter-independent exactly when their sums agree.

But Eq. (15) at \(N=1\) fixes the coefficient of a changed observation as \(\theta/(\sigma^2+\tau^2)\), while \(N=2\) requires \(\theta/(\sigma^2+2\tau^2)\). The same \(\eta,S\) cannot supply both. Base measures and normalizers cancel in this comparison, even if the statistic dimension is enlarged.
checks.repair:
Replace the exhaustive exponential-family characterization by the general sufficiency factorization

\[
p(X_N\mid\theta)=h_N(X_N)G_N\!\left(\theta,\sum_i t^*(x_i)\right).
\]

A useful sufficient condition for the stronger common exponential-family form is the pre-integration conditional kernel

\[
p(x\mid\theta,\psi)=h(x)\exp\!\left[\eta(\theta)^TT(x)+\xi(\psi)^TU(x)-a(\theta)-b(\psi)\right],
\]

with a parameter-independent nuisance prior and finite positive integrals. Integrating the one shared nuisance gives

\[
p(X_N\mid\theta)=H_N(X_N)\exp\!\left[\eta(\theta)^T\sum_iT(x_i)-Na(\theta)\right],
\]

where

\[
H_N(X_N)=\left(\prod_i h(x_i)\right)\int p(\psi)\exp\!\left[\xi(\psi)^T\sum_iU(x_i)-Nb(\psi)\right]d\psi
\]

is independent of \(\theta\). If the natural-parameter differences span the statistic space, its sum is also minimal sufficient.

For example, separate channels \(a_i\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)\) and \(b_i\mid\psi\sim N(\psi,1)\) retain genuine shared-nuisance dependence and satisfy this condition. The original common exponential-family necessity claim must be removed. An additive conditional natural parameter alone does not separate its normalizer.
checks.scope: The repaired sufficient condition is on the conditional kernel before integration, rather than assuming Eq. (15). The main mean-pool theorem may still use assumption (M) directly; its other steps are not certified here. Allowing a set-size-dependent natural parameter fixes the Gaussian example but is not a general characterization.
checks.title: Shared-nuisance sufficiency does not force one exponential form across set sizes
checks.whyItMatters: The proposed exponential-family restriction on mean-pool inference excludes a regular model that already has a one-dimensional sufficient mean.
checks.claimContext: Corollary 2 claims that a fixed additive minimal sufficient statistic for the shared-nuisance marginal forces Eq. (15) with both the statistic and natural-parameter map independent of set size.

checks.claim: All globally optimal encoders are affine-equivalent to one another.
checks.explanation: An affine projection to a common statistic need not be invertible. Optimal encoders can carry irrelevant coordinates that are not affinely related while yielding the same exact posterior.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(x=(a,b)\), with \(a\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)\) and independent \(b\sim N(0,1)\), and use a full-support prior. The sample mean of \(a\) is minimal sufficient at every set size. Choose

\[
t_1(a,b)=(a,b),\qquad t_2(a,b)=(a,b^3).
\]

Both are homeomorphisms onto \(\mathbb R^2\), meeting the continuity, quotient-map and nonempty-interior conditions. A universal head ignores the second pooled coordinate and recovers the exact posterior at every allowed training size.

No affine map sends \(b\) to \(b^3\) on \(\mathbb R\), nor does an affine inverse exist. Nevertheless both recover the same minimal statistic through the rectangular projection

\[
t^*(x)=a=(1,0)t_1(x)=(1,0)t_2(x).
\]

Thus common affine recovery does not make the full encoders invertibly affine-equivalent.
checks.repair: Retain the conclusion that each encoder has an affine projection to the common minimal sufficient statistic and hence supports the same posterior. To claim affine equivalence of the complete embeddings, additionally require square nonsingular recovery matrices. Then \(t_2=A_2^{-1}A_1t_1+A_2^{-1}(b_1-b_2)\) is an invertible affine relation.
checks.scope: The counterexample meets the inherited support, image, optimality and minimal-statistic hypotheses. It refutes full-encoder equivalence, not the retained posterior sufficiency conclusion.
checks.title: Optimal encoders can differ in nonlinear ancillary coordinates
checks.whyItMatters: Posterior sufficiency constrains recoverable information; the stronger equivalence would also constrain irrelevant coordinates.
checks.claimContext: Corollary 3 claims invertible affine equivalence of full globally optimal encoders. Its preceding recovery result only gives \(t^*(x)=A_it_i(x)+b_i\), where \(A_i\) may be rectangular.

The key observation that makes the depth-overhead P_D = O(D^2) work is Lemma 3.5: the recursive product prod_{j=i+1}^D (1 + Lambda_pre/alpha_j) is bounded because for alpha_j = (j+1)^2, sum_j 1/(j+1)^2 < infinity, so the infinite product converges to a constant depending only on Lambda_pre. Combined with max_{i<=D}(1+alpha_i) = O(D^2), this gives P_D = O_{Lambda_pre, Lambda_gap}(D^2). The active-call localization in Proposition B.10 is also clean: the per-edge cap k_i <= k_{i-1} ensures rho_{k_{i-1}} <= rho_{k_i}, and the max recursion Delta_{x_i}^{eff} = max{Delta_{x_{i-1}}^{eff}, |V*(x_i) - V*(x_{i-1})|} is bounded by max{2 rho_{k_{i-1}}, rho_{k_i}} <= 2 rho_{k_i}, giving C_act(D) = 2 (depth-independent). The biased-slow-oracle extension (Theorem 3.7) is also tight: the inflation by xi (not 2 xi or more) works because the slow sample's mean is V*(v) + b_v with |b_v| <= xi, so widening the slow confidence radius by xi absorbs the bias; the bound does not accumulate with depth because each level of recursion has the same fixed offset xi, not a per-level additive bias. Theorem 3.8 (loose fast-oracle envelope) is straightforward: hat B(h) >= B(h) means I_v^F widens, so I_v^loc may be wider but is still valid. The truncated Theorem 3.6 full proof is in Appendix B.6 which was cut off in the file; I verified the proof sketch in the main text and all building-block lemmas (B.2-B.14) but could not check the very end of the proof. The algorithm pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-5) is consistent with the analysis. The only thing I did not numerically verify is the experimental Table 1 numbers (which are reported, not derived).
